extracted_by: hand, T-0315 — the Democrat read, June 1834
note: Vol. I No. 30, the last number of Volume I and the last issue of T-0258's thirty. Page 3 columns 1-2 are the fresh advertising and are NOT interleaved; columns 3-6 and the whole of page 4 are, and badly — this issue carries 266 uncertainty markers, the most of the four. Pages 1-2 are the Bank controversy and the Illinois-Michigan boundary argument. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST: all twenty-four columns were read, not searched. THE ISSUE'S OWN NEWS is a school, a Fourth of July meeting, two new firms and the Indian Agent's removal notice, all datelined 20-25 June and none of them in the previous week's paper.

claims.notes: A BUILDING PLACED BY ANOTHER BUILDING, AND BOTH ARE ON THE GROUND: a school opening on Monday 30 June 1834 'on Randolph[-street], in a building nearly in rear of the Presbyterian Church, between Clark and Dearborn'. That fixes the Presbyterian Church to the Randolph block between Clark and Dearborn and puts a second structure behind it, which is the only backlot building the June reading finds. The school itself is one of the seventy-five raised this spring or an existing room taken over — the notice does not say which. THE MISTRESS ARRIVED FROM EDINBURGH within weeks of advertising, which is the emigration the same month's editorial describes, at the scale of one person. The surname is 'WATITB' in the heading and is read Waite; no forename is printed, and 'Miss Waite' is minted as it stands rather than guessed at.

claims.notes: A THIRD NAME FOR THE SAME HOUSE. The Board of Trustees met 'at the house of E. Haddock' on 6 June (1834-06-18 claim c002); a lot is sold 'one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street' on 18 June (that issue's claim c006); and here the citizens are called to 'H. Haddock's Mansion House' on 25 June. Tavern, house and Mansion House are the same establishment named three ways in three weeks, and the initial is E. once and H. twice — a reading this pass records and does not resolve, because 'Haddock's Mansion House' on Lake Street is placeable whichever initial is right. THE MEETING IS THE TOWN'S PUBLIC ASSEMBLY ROOM in practice: a tavern is where Chicago's civic business happened in 1834.

claims.notes: THE SUCCESSOR TO THE FIRM DISSOLVED ON 5 MAY, and it names the building: 'the old shop formerly [occupied by] Pierce and Abbott' (the dissolution is 1834-06-11 claim c003). So a blacksmith's shop that existed before May 1834 is still standing and working in late June under a new partnership — a continuity of STRUCTURE, not just of trade, which is what a reconstruction needs. THE CORNER IS HALF-READ. The line gives '...al streets' and the interleaving takes the first street name; Canal is the only street in the plat ending in 'al' and is read with confidence, its partner is not read at all, and 'opposite the Chicago [—]' loses its object the same way. So the placement is recorded as a corner on Canal Street with the anchor stated as far as the page carries it and a dash where the paper is unreadable. Nothing is invented to fill either gap. French's forename is not printed.

claims.notes: RULING 3'S VETO, TWENTY-FIVE DAYS AFTER THE FIRM ADVERTISED ITS OPENING. Tuttle & Brown announce a new store one door south of Newberry & Dole on 27 May (1834-06-04 claim c011) and dissolve on 21 June, with J. B. Tuttle continuing alone. THE STAND IS NOT NAMED IN THIS NOTICE — the placement carried here is the opening advertisement's and is bracketed as such in the offset field, so the dissolution and the address stay attached to the same business record without this claim pretending to state an address it does not. A grocery that lasted under four weeks is worth its own note about how fast this town's storefronts changed hands in 1834.

claims.notes: THE TREATY OF CHICAGO ENFORCED FROM AN OFFICE IN THE TOWN, thirteen months before the scene date and by the same man who signs the town ordinances as president of the Board of Trustees (1834-06-18 claim c004). The notice states the three-year retention north of the Illinois line and orders every settler off the ceded lands within thirty days, and a second paragraph permits Indians who have planted on the ceded land inside the state to stay 'until they shall have harvested their crops'. PLANTED FIELDS INSIDE THE STATE IN JUNE 1834 is a fact about the ground this reconstruction covers, stated by the official whose business it was to know. The removal it enforces is the reason the 1835 town looks the way it does, and it belongs in the record as the Agency printed it.
